READY

1. A reversible installation begins with a documented baseline of the system state before any change is made, because reversal is only verifiable if you know what "before" looked like. Record package inventories, configuration checksums, listening ports, and service statuses in a dated snapshot file stored outside the affected tree. For example, on a Fedora box you might run `rpm -qa > pre-install-rpms.txt`, `sha256sum /etc/nginx/nginx.conf >> baseline-checksums.txt`, and `ss -tlnp > pre-install-ports.txt` before touching anything.

2. The installation itself should be performed through a package manager rather than a tarball dumped into /usr/local, because package managers keep an install manifest that doubles as an uninstall script. Verify reversibility by confirming the transaction log records every file the installer touched. For example, installing with `sudo dnf install --setopt=tsflags=nodocs postgresql-server` leaves the exact file list in the RPM database, and `rpm -ql postgresql-server` can enumerate it later for verification against what actually landed on disk.

3. If you must install from source, redirect every artifact into a self-contained prefix so that removal is a single directory operation with no stray files. Configure the build with an explicit prefix such as `/opt/widget-1.4.2` rather than the default system paths. For example, `./configure --prefix=/opt/widget-1.4.2 && make && make install` keeps binaries, libraries, and man pages under one versioned directory, and `make -n install` run beforehand shows you the install manifest so you can verify nothing escapes the prefix.

4. Configuration reversibility means distinguishing files the installer will overwrite from files the administrator owns, and proving the difference with timestamps and copies. Before editing, copy each config to a versioned backup directory and record its checksum. For example, before enabling TLS you would run `sudo cp -a /etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf /etc/backup/2026-10-05/app.conf.orig`, then after your edit verify with `diff` that only intended lines changed, and confirm reversal works by restoring the copy and re-running `nginx -t`.

5. Configuration changes should be introduced incrementally with a verification step between each, so a failed change can be pinpointed and reverted surgically. Each verification is a command with a clear pass criterion, not a subjective glance at logs. For example, after adding a reverse-proxy block you run `sudo nginx -t`, expect `syntax is ok` and `test is successful`, and if a later change makes the test fail you revert exactly one block with `cp /etc/backup/2026-10-05/app.conf.orig /etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf` and confirm the test passes again.

6. Dependency verification means proving that the package manager's dependency graph is complete and that removing the top-level package will not orphan or remove things other software needs. Inspect reverse dependencies before assuming removal is safe. For example, before planning to remove `libxml2` as part of uninstalling a parser tool, run `dnf repoquery --whatrequires libxml2` and discover that `rpm` itself depends on it, which tells you the dependency is system-shared and must not be part of the reversal scope.

7. Vendored or pinned dependencies deserve their own isolation check, because a shared library installed for one app can silently break another when reversed. Verify that private dependencies live in a namespace the reversal cannot reach by accident. For example, a Python app installed with `python3 -m venv /opt/etl/venv` keeps its pinned `requests==2.31.0` inside the virtualenv, so `rm -rf /opt/etl/venv` reverses cleanly, whereas a `sudo pip3 install requests` written to the system site-packages could collide with another tool using the same name and must be reversed with `pip3 uninstall` plus a verification that the other tool still imports.

8. Shared-library installations need explicit linker-path verification so you can prove the reversal restores the previous resolution order. Record how the loader resolves the library before and after installation. For example, run `ldd /opt/widget-1.4.2/bin/widget | grep libssl` before and after adding a line to `/etc/ld.so.conf.d/widget.conf`; after reversal, remove the file, run `sudo ldconfig -p | grep libssl` to confirm the old path is resolved again, and re-run `ldd` to prove the binary is back on the system library.

9. Permission verification means capturing the pre-install ownership and mode of every directory the software will write to, then diffing after installation to detect drift. Reversal is not complete if a directory the daemon created under `0777` survives the uninstall. For example, snapshot `/var/lib` and `/var/log` with `getfacl -R /var/lib/myapp > pre-install-acl.txt`, install the package which creates `/var/lib/myapp` owned by the `myapp` user, and after removal verify with `find /var/lib -name myapp` that nothing remains and that no world-writable artifacts were left behind.

10. Service-account and capability changes must be enumerated so the reversal removes the principal itself, not just the software it ran. Document account details before deletion, because a deleted account's numeric UID can otherwise linger in orphaned files. For example, the installer creates a system user via `sudo useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin -d /var/lib/myapp myapp`; record its UID with `id myapp`, and verify reversal by confirming `getent passwd myapp` returns nothing and that `find / -nouser -uid 993 2>/dev/null` reports no files still owned by the gone account.

11. Verify that permission changes were scoped to the software's paths by testing neighboring paths for unintended modification. A chmod applied too broadly is a common reversal trap. For example, if the installer ran `chmod -R 775 /opt/widget-1.4.2` and you later discover a careless variant hit `/opt` itself, `find /opt -perm /002 -o -perm -g+w | grep -v widget` shows collateral damage, and the corrected reversal is `sudo chmod -R g-w /opt/widget-1.4.2` limited strictly to the software's own tree with a second sweep to prove `/opt` and other apps were untouched.

12. Service restart verification requires proving both that the running service reflects the new state and that the previous version can be restarted cleanly after reversal. Never treat "systemctl status shows active" as sufficient. For example, after upgrading `myapp` you run `sudo systemctl restart myapp && systemctl show myapp -p ExecMainStartTimestamp,MainPID` to capture the fresh process identity, and as a reversal rehearsal you stop the new unit, start the old unit file kept at `/etc/systemd/system/myapp@1.3.0.service`, confirm `curl -s localhost:8080/healthz` reports version 1.3.0, then switch forward again.

13. Restart verification also covers graceful shutdown behavior under load, because an uninstall that assumes clean shutdown can corrupt state if the process ignores signals. Test the drain path with synthetic traffic before trusting it. For example, generate ten slow requests with `for i in $(seq 10); curl -s localhost:8080/slow-report & done`, then issue `sudo systemctl restart myapp` and confirm the journal shows `systemd[1]: Stopping myapp.service...` followed by completion within the unit's `TimeoutStopSec=30` rather than a `SIGKILL` after 90 seconds of stonewalling.

14. Interruption verification means deliberately interrupting the installation at each phase and confirming the system can be returned to baseline from that exact point. Test this on a clone or disposable VM first, never the production host. For example, run `sudo rpm -i widget-1.4.2.rpm` and kill the process mid-transaction with `sudo pkill -9 rpm` during the scriptlet phase, then verify the recovery path: `sudo rpm --rebuilddb && sudo rpm -e --noscripts widget-1.4.2 && diff <(rpm -qa | sort) pre-install-rpms.txt` shows the package set back identical to baseline.

15. Interruption during configuration and data migration deserves its own test, because half-applied migrations are the classic case where naive rollback makes things worse. Verify the tool supports checkpointed or transactional migrations. For example, interrupt a Django upgrade mid-`migrate` with Ctrl-C at the migration named `0047_add_invoice_index`, then confirm reversal with `python manage.py migrate 0046_auto_20260912`, inspecting `SHOW INDEX FROM invoices` to prove the partial index is gone and re-running `python manage.py migrate --check` to prove schema state matches the models.

16. Backup verification for a reversible installation is not "a backup file exists" but "a backup restored successfully at least once." A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not an asset. For example, after `sudo tar czf /backup/etc-2026-10-05.tar.gz /etc`, verify integrity with `tar tzf /backup/etc-2026-10-05.tar.gz | wc -l` compared against `find /etc -type f | wc -l`, and rehearse the restore in a throwaway loop with `mkdir /tmp/restore && tar xzf /backup/etc-2026-10-05.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore` followed by a spot `diff -r /tmp/restore/etc/ssh /etc/ssh`.

17. Backup scope must include the configuration deltas the installer makes, not just user data, or the rollback will restore data onto the wrong configuration. Capture deltas with a mechanism that survives host failure. For example, keep `/etc` under a local git repository: `git -C /etc commit -am "pre widget-1.4.2 baseline"` before installing, so the reversal is `git -C /etc checkout pre-baseline-tag -- /etc/nginx` and the push to a private remote is what you test first, because a delta backup that lives only on the machine being rolled back is not a backup.

18. Application data backup verification requires a restore drill at the application level, since a restored file the application cannot open is worthless. Verify with the application's own tooling. For example, back up Postgres with `pg_dump -Fc mydb > mydb-pre-upgrade.dump`, rehearse the rollback on a scratch instance with `pg_restore -d mydb_rehearsal mydb-pre-upgrade.dump`, and verify not just success but equivalence: row counts per table and a checksummed `SELECT md5(string_agg(name)) FROM customers` matching the source before you trust the dump for a real downgrade from version 16 to 15.

19. User data protection during installation means verifying the software does not rewrite, normalize, or relocate files owned by users, and that reversal restores anything it did. Take a content-addressed manifest of user data before installing. For example, build `find /srv/uploads -type f -exec sha256sum {} + > uploads-baseline.sha256`, run the installer's data migration, then `sha256sum -c uploads-baseline.sha256` to prove byte-for-byte immutability; if the migration legitimately transforms data, the baseline file is your proof of what rollback must restore and the checksum list doubles as its instruction sheet.

20. User-data reversibility also requires verifying that database records referencing deleted assets are reversible, which is where backups alone fall short. Check referential integrity after any restore into a changed schema. For example, after restoring a backup from before the widget-1.4.2 install onto a schema that still expects the new `avatar_id` column, run `SELECT count(*) FROM profiles WHERE avatar_id IS NOT NULL` and `psql -c "REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW"` style integrity checks; if the restore fails, your verification has proven that schema rollback and data rollback must be sequenced together, which is exactly what a rehearsal is for.

21. Rollback verification means executing the full reversal once, on a non-production copy, and diffing the end state against the pre-install baseline rather than trusting the uninstaller's exit code. Define the acceptance criterion as an empty diff. For example, run `sudo dnf remove widget-1.4.2 && systemctl status widget && ss -tlnp`, then compare `dnf repoquery --installed > post-uninstall-rpms.txt && diff post-uninstall-rpms.txt pre-install-rpms.txt`, expecting no output, and grep the journal for leftover units before declaring the rollback real.

22. Rollback verification for source installs means proving the prefix removal leaves no residue in shared locations. Search every shared path the build could have touched. For example, after `rm -rf /opt/widget-1.4.2`, run `sudo ldconfig && ldconfig -p | grep widget` expecting nothing, `grep -r widget /etc/ld.so.conf.d/ /usr/lib/systemd/system/ 2>/dev/null` expecting nothing, and `sudo updatedb && locate widget | grep -v /opt` expecting only the removed prefix's log entries, then decide whether `/var/log/widget` is intentionally kept as evidence.

23. A full rehearsal of the rollback under time pressure is the final gate, because a reversal that takes six hours of confused effort is not effectively reversible. Time the end-to-end drill and write the steps into a runbook with expected outputs. For example, on a staging clone timed with `time ./rollback-widget.sh`, the script stops the service, restores the `mydb-pre-upgrade.dump`, reverts `/etc` from the git tag, removes the RPM, and restarts; the drill passes when it finishes in under fifteen minutes and the post-drill checks from the previous paragraphs all return their expected empty diffs and version strings.

24. Reversibility verification is not complete until a second person can execute the rollback from the runbook alone, because the installer's mental model is not documentation. Hand the runbook, baselines, and staging host to a colleague who did not do the install, and stay out of the room. For example, when your colleague runs `dnf remove widget-1.4.2`, restores the config from `/etc` git history, rehearses the database restore, and reports a clean `diff` against `pre-install-rpms.txt` and matching `sha256sum -c uploads-baseline.sha256` results without calling you, the installation is verified reversible; capture their stumbling points as runbook fixes, then schedule a re-verification before each subsequent upgrade.
